intro: I'm Moataz, a mechanical engineering senior at Boston University. My main interests are robotics, R&D, 3D printing, and electromechanical design.
The projects I like most need a CAD model, a circuit board, and a test plan to all work together. This site shows the ones I'm proud of and what I learned building them.

about.heading: About

projects.title: Flint
projects.card: A gym wearable that estimates how close you are to muscle failure. Custom PCB, snap-fit housing, and a phone app.
projects.summary: A wearable that estimates how close a lifter is to muscle failure. I designed the circuit board and the housing, then built the app around them.

cover.alt: Flint prototype glowing red on its charger

steps.title: Problem
body: Lifters have no objective way to tell how close a set is to muscle failure, one of the key drivers of strength and muscle growth.

steps.title: Approach
body: My first idea was EMG on the working muscle. Electrodes were hard to secure and remove, and most muscles are covered by clothing.
I switched to velocity-based training (VBT), which estimates fatigue from how the weight moves. That set three requirements:
bullets: A low-noise 6-axis IMU to measure acceleration and angular velocity
A phone app connection to process and display the data
Mounting that lets the IMU track the weight's movement

steps.title: Electronics
body: A wearable has to be compact to be comfortable, so a custom PCB was non-negotiable. I designed two revisions and hand-soldered every SMD and through-hole part.
Rev 2 fixed most of rev 1's problems and needed only a few bodge wires.
steps.note: Lesson: plan for rotating parts, LEDs, and ports from day one.

items.alt: Schematic of the first Flint PCB
Schematic of the redesigned Flint PCB
First Flint PCB, assembled and powered with a battery attached
Second Flint PCB, smaller, with LEDs lit

steps.title: Housing
body: Three parts: bottom overmold, top overmold, and dial. I exported the PCB as a 3D model and designed the housing around it.

The PCB and battery slide into the bottom half and the top half locks them in. With 2 mm walls, the snap-fits were the hard part. I ended up with four button-tipped tabs and a center dovetail that guides everything into place.

items.cap: PCB and battery seated in the bottom overmold
items.alt: CAD view of the Flint PCB inside the bottom housing
CAD close-up of the snap-fit tabs on the Flint housing

steps.title: Assembly and app
body: I assembled the device with a custom velcro strap and built a phone app around it.

The app's GymScore ring combines several metrics, half of them straight from the device. A device tab updates the firmware from the phone, and a live workout view counts reps and analyzes failure. That view is still in progress. A workout can also be started from the dial on the device.

items.alt: Flint housing, strap, battery, dial, and PCB laid out on a box
Flint wearable strapped to the back of a hand
Flint wearable glowing white while charging
Flint app home screen with a GymScore of 54
Flint app device screen showing battery, live IMU data, and firmware status
Flint app live workout screen counting 10 reps

projects.title: C.H.I.P
projects.card: A smaller, controller-driven rebuild of our hackathon robot, with a clear resin shell for a future camera.
projects.summary: A smaller, controller-driven rebuild of our hackathon-winning spherical robot, with a clear shell for a future camera.

cover.alt: C.H.I.P robot with its clear shell next to a game controller

steps.title: Goal
body: Take H.A.M.S.T.E.R., the robot my team built in a 24-hour hackathon, and refine it. I wanted three changes: a smaller body so it deploys more easily, Bluetooth controller support, and a more polished design.

steps.title: Shrink the core
body: The hackathon robot fastened everything to a laser-cut plate. I replaced it with a custom 3D printed core that packs every component into a smaller footprint.

items.cap: Inner core, which houses the electronics and weights
items.alt: CAD model of the C.H.I.P inner core
C.H.I.P inner core with wheels and electronics, held inside half of the shell

steps.title: Balance it
body: Testing showed that the real problem was center of mass. If it does not sit below the point where the wheels touch the shell, the core spins inside the shell and the robot goes nowhere.
I weighed, adjusted, and retested until the design drove reliably.
steps.note: Mass too high and it just spins in place.

steps.title: Clear shell
body: I made two shells: one printed in white PETG and one in clear resin. I sanded the resin shell and sprayed it with several finishing coats to get it as transparent as possible, so a future camera can see through it for teleoperation.

items.alt: Resin shell half curing under blue UV light
Clear resin shell half drying on cardboard

steps.title: Controller
body: I updated the firmware on the ESP32 for wireless control, then wrote code that maps joystick input to the independent rotation of each motor. The result is smooth, responsive driving.

steps.title: Result
body: A compact, rugged search vehicle with controller support, a clear shell ready for a camera feed, and shells that swap for different jobs.

items.cap: Driving C.H.I.P with the Bluetooth controller

projects.title: H.A.M.S.T.E.R.
projects.kicker: Hazardous Area Mobility and Search Technology for Emergency Response
projects.card: A spherical search and rescue robot built in 24 hours. 1st place overall at MakeHarvard.
projects.summary: A spherical search and rescue robot built in 24 hours at MakeHarvard. Our team took 1st place overall.

cover.alt: H.A.M.S.T.E.R. spherical robot with a black perforated shell and yellow band

steps.title: Problem
body: Natural disasters are becoming more frequent and more intense, and hazardous conditions can delay search operations for days. One of my teammates saw that firsthand during the California wildfires.
We wanted a robust, nimble robot that could search dangerous areas for survivors remotely.

steps.title: Concept
body: A sphere. The outer shell protects the electronics and rolls over rough terrain, a low center of mass keeps the robot from flipping, and the whole thing is small enough to deploy quickly and drive from a phone.

steps.title: Inner core
body: Everything mounts to a 12 cm x 12 cm laser-cut base. I made custom holders for the motors, and the wheels point outward near the middle of the body instead of sitting underneath. Inside a sphere, they still reach the shell.
Weights under the base lower the center of mass so the core self-stabilizes.

items.alt: Robot inner core with two wheels, motors, and a microcontroller

steps.title: Outer shell
body: Two 3D printed halves in black PLA. We had no transparent filament, so we added holes instead. As the shell spins, the camera's frame rate blurs them into a see-through view, like looking past a spinning fan.

items.alt: Two black perforated shell halves on a cutting mat

steps.title: Result
body: 1st place overall. We also designed and tested a camera and air quality sensors, but ran out of time to integrate them with the drive code.

items.alt: Four teammates standing in front of a screen that reads First Place

projects.title: SolidWorks
projects.card: Part modeling from engineering drawings, motion studies that check my hand calcs, and FEA.
projects.summary: How I use SolidWorks: modeling parts from engineering drawings, running motion studies to check hand calculations, and using FEA to find weak spots before anything gets made.
facts: Part modeling, Hole Wizard, Motion, Simulation

cover.alt: Engineering drawing of a gauge block with section and isometric views

steps.title: Modeling from drawings
body: In my Intro to CAD class, each project starts with an engineering drawing that I read and recreate as a model.

items.cap: Model 1, built around the revolve feature. Three hours to read the drawing, plan the build, and recreate the model and its drawing.
items.alt: Engineering drawing of a revolved fitting

items.cap: Model 2, a more complex drawing. Hole Wizard handled the counterbored, countersunk, and tapped holes.
items.alt: Engineering drawing of a gauge block with multiple hole types

steps.title: Motion studies
body: I use motion studies to check calculations before building. For a rod-carrying cart, one study confirmed my hand-calculated tipping acceleration and a second confirmed that the velocity profile covers 10 feet. For a 4-bar linkage, I pulled motor torque and bearing reaction forces from the study.

steps.title: FEA
body: For a bell rocket nozzle, a teammate and I ran FEA at our calculated pressures. The first design was too thin in places, so I revised it and tested it again at a factor of safety of 2.

items.cap: Stress results at a factor of safety of 2
items.alt: FEA stress plot of a rocket nozzle
Rocket nozzle model with fixture locations marked

projects.title: CoreXY Whack-A-Mole
projects.kicker: A game with one very fast mole
projects.card: One mole on a CoreXY gantry travels to a hole, pops up, and dares you to hit it.
projects.summary: A whack-a-mole game where a single mole physically travels to a hole on a CoreXY gantry, then pops up. Hit it three times and you win.
facts: Team project, ME 360 at Boston University
Concept pitch, mole mechanism, top panel, button wiring

cover.alt: Whack-a-mole game with a green painted top panel and a green mole with a red button

steps.title: Brief
body: Design a 2.5 degree-of-freedom device with a clear purpose. I pitched a whack-a-mole game where the mole chooses a hole, travels to it, and pops up. You have to hit it while it is extended. Catch it three times and you win.

items.alt: Whiteboard sketch of the gantry and mole mechanism

steps.title: Frame
body: We started by getting the basic gantry layout fixed together.

items.alt: Aluminum extrusion gantry frame with red printed brackets

steps.title: Mole mechanism
body: I designed the rack and pinion that raises the mole. My first version had nowhere to mount the button, and the solid mole made the assembly too front-heavy.
The redesign hollowed out the mole and added a button mount.

items.cap: Version 1: no button mount, too front-heavy
items.alt: CAD model of the first mole and rack design

items.cap: First print test of the redesigned mole

steps.title: Top panel
body: I designed the fixture for the wooden top panel, laser cut and positioned the holes, painted it, and wired the button on the mole.

items.alt: Unpainted wooden panel with five holes and the mole in the center
Painted green and blue panel mounted on the gantry

steps.title: Result
body: The finished game, with the mole picking holes on its own.

projects.title: Retro Mechanical Doorbell
projects.kicker: Programmable tunes on a real drum
projects.card: A doorbell that plays programmable tunes on a real drum, using one solenoid and one servo.
projects.summary: A doorbell that plays programmable tunes on a real drum. Built for a client brief that asked for a retro look, a mechanical sound, and modern features.
facts: Team of 4, course project with a sample client
Sound mechanism concept, drum mounts, inner housing

cover.alt: Laser-cut wooden doorbell housing with an engraved rose

steps.title: Client brief
body: A sample client asked for a retro doorbell with a mechanically actuated sound and modern features. It also had to be pet-friendly and inclusive to use.
We ranked our objectives with a pairwise comparison chart and defined a test for each one:
bullets: A loud, pleasant mechanical tune, between 60 and 70 dB
A retro look, reminiscent of the 1960s
Activation that does not depend on most senses or appendages, with sound below 25,000 Hz

steps.title: Concept
body: The hardest part was a mechanical sound source that could play different pre-programmed songs. My idea was a rain drum, a small drum with several notes.
A solenoid strikes the drum, and a continuous servo rotates it to bring each note under the striker.

steps.title: Mount, version 1
body: My first mount held the drum well. Too well. The tight grip damped the vibration and muted the sound.

items.cap: Version 1 damped the sound too much

steps.title: Mount, version 2
body: I needed to hold the drum firmly while touching as little of it as possible. The drain hole in the bottom of the drum solved it. A tight-tolerance part grips the drum from the inside and leaves the surface free to ring.

items.cap: Version 2: simpler, and a better fit

steps.title: Integration
body: I designed the inner housing that holds every part in place, with a compartment for the electronics under the servo. My teammates tied the solenoid and servo circuit to an infrared sensor, and everything went into a prototype enclosure.

items.cap: The mechanism inside the prototype housing

steps.title: Result
body: The finished doorbell, playing its tune.

items.alt: Laser-cut wooden doorbell housing with an engraved rose

projects.title: Hidden Bike Tracker
projects.kicker: An AirTag mount nobody can find
projects.card: A 3D printed AirTag mount that hides in plain sight. Designed, printed, and installed in 4 hours.
projects.summary: A 3D printed AirTag mount that hides in plain sight on my bike. Designed, printed, and installed in 4 hours.

cover.alt: Underside of a bike with an arrow pointing to the hidden tracker mount

steps.title: Problem
body: I wanted to check my bike's location from my phone at any time. An AirTag does that, but only if nobody notices it.

steps.title: Design
body: I had spare black filament, so I picked a black part of the bike and an existing screw to mount to.
The mount installs upside down, so I modeled it inverted. Once it is on the bike, the lid sits on top and the AirTag never rests on it, which keeps the lid from opening and the tag from falling out.
After a lot of measuring and several test prints, it fit.

items.alt: CAD model of the AirTag mount with its lid

steps.title: Test
body: I asked a friend to find it. A few minutes of searching turned up nothing. Even after I flipped over the part of the bike it hides on, the black enclosure blended in and was hard to spot.

projects.title: E-Bike Trunk
projects.card: A two-door trunk for my e-bike's rack, split in half to fit the printer and snapped back together.
projects.summary: A two-door trunk for my e-bike's rear rack. I chose the manufacturing process first, then designed every part around it.

cover.alt: White 3D printed trunk with black lids mounted on an e-bike rack

steps.title: Problem
body: I ride an e-bike to get around and was tired of wearing a backpack every time I had to carry something. The bike came with a metal rear rack, so I planned a trunk I could throw things into and close.

items.alt: E-bike with a bare rear rack and a handwritten note that says trunk needed

steps.title: Plan around the process
body: I picked the manufacturing process first: my Bambu A1 printer. Then I sketched the concept, measured the rack, and rebuilt it in CAD so I could design the mount against it.
The mount combines a tight diagonal fit with screw holes.

steps.title: Too big to print
body: The trunk was larger than my print bed. I split the body into two halves that snap-fit together.

steps.title: Lids
body: My first idea was a single thin lid that opened like a garage door. It turned out to be impractical. I switched to two doors with a hinge on each side, so either half opens on its own.
I test printed hinges at several tolerances before settling on the final fit.

items.alt: CAD model of the trunk with two lids

steps.title: Result
body: Four printed parts. The body halves are white PETG and took about 36 hours each. The lids are black PLA, and one deformed on a hot day.
It has been a convenient, functional addition to my bike.

items.alt: Trunk mounted on the bike with both lids closed
Trunk mounted on the bike with one lid open

projects.title: Rod Transport Cart
projects.card: Carries a free-standing rod 10 feet and back without tipping it. Hand calcs, simulation, build, test.
projects.summary: A cart that carries a free-standing metal rod 10 feet and back as fast as possible without tipping it. Calculated by hand, verified in simulation, then built and tested.
facts: Team project, ME 360 at Boston University

cover.alt: Wooden cart with four laser-cut wheels and an Arduino on top

steps.title: Brief
body: Move a metal rod standing on top of a cart 10 feet and back, as fast as possible, without knocking it over. That takes two things: a cart, and the fastest velocity profile the rod can survive.

steps.title: Hand calculations
body: I calculated the maximum acceleration the rod can take before it topples, then mapped that limit to a velocity profile that covers 10 feet.

steps.title: Verify in simulation
body: I rebuilt the setup in SolidWorks, applied the velocity profile, and measured the reaction force on the rod below, at, and above my calculated limit. The reaction force only reached zero at the calculated value, which confirmed the hand calc.
I also checked the assembly's degrees of freedom so the study could be trusted.

items.cap: Velocity input for the limit case
items.alt: SolidWorks function builder showing a linear velocity ramp

items.cap: Reaction force on the rod over time
items.alt: Plot of reaction force versus time

steps.title: Size the drivetrain
body: The motor tops out at 240 rpm. I calculated the wheel size needed to follow the velocity profile, programmed it into the rotary motor, and ran the study. The cart reached the maximum acceleration and traveled the full 10 feet.

items.cap: Velocity profile for the full run
items.alt: SolidWorks function builder showing a triangular velocity profile

items.cap: Motion study of the 10 foot run

steps.title: Motor control
body: The DC motor runs from an Arduino through an amplifier on a 12 V supply.

items.cap: Arduino, amplifier, and motor on the bench
items.alt: Arduino wired to a motor driver and DC motor
Arduino code for driving the motor forward and backward

steps.title: Build
body: My team and I cut the plywood deck, 3D printed custom axle and motor fixtures, laser cut and sanded the wheels, wired the electronics, and programmed the profile.

items.alt: Laser cutter cutting wheel parts
Wooden cart with electronics mounted on top

steps.title: Test
body: We ran the cart several times and tuned it between runs.

projects.title: Neodymium Siphon Design Report
projects.kicker: One week from zero to a full design report
projects.card: A design report for harvesting molten neodymium from an electrolytic cell.
projects.summary: A design report for a siphon system that harvests molten neodymium from an electrolytic cell. Researched, modeled, and written in one week.

steps.title: What the report covers
bullets: A detailed system diagram with annotated components and materials
Mathematical models that optimize flow rate and efficiency
Climate considerations and material choices that address sustainability and safety

steps.title: What I had to learn
body: To write it, I taught myself the basics of fluid dynamics, thermodynamics, electrolytic cells, and the material properties of neodymium, plus Adobe Illustrator for the system diagram.

projects.title: Rocket Nozzle
projects.card: A bell nozzle sized from first principles, modeled in CAD, and checked with FEA.
projects.summary: A bell nozzle designed with BU Rocket Propulsion Group: sized from first principles, modeled in CAD, and checked with FEA.
facts: Team project, BU Rocket Propulsion Group

cover.alt: CAD render of a bell rocket nozzle with a bolted flange

steps.title: Learn
body: New members of BU Rocket Propulsion Group spend their first semester in a crash course on rocket science that ends with a team nozzle design. I spent two months in a rocketry textbook learning specific impulse, thrust, and the geometry that sets them.

steps.title: Calculate
body: A teammate and I independently solved for 12 design parameters for a given fuel and set of operating conditions.

items.alt: Spreadsheet of nozzle design parameters in metric and imperial units

steps.title: Model
body: I modeled the nozzle in CAD from those parameters, using a bell nozzle design.

items.alt: CAD model of the bell nozzle

steps.title: Analyze
body: A teammate and I ran FEA at our calculated pressures. The first design was too thin in some areas, so I modified it until it was ready to manufacture.

items.cap: Tests with a factor of safety of 2
items.alt: FEA stress plot of the nozzle
Nozzle model with fixture locations marked

steps.title: Result
body: The club was not able to manufacture the new-member nozzles for a test fire that semester, because of supply issues and its larger project, Icarus. I still came away with a working understanding of nozzle design from equations to analysis.

projects.title: Heart Rate Monitor
projects.card: A speaker used in reverse as a pulse sensor, amplified with a cascade of op-amps.
projects.summary: A heart rate monitor that uses a speaker as the sensor and a cascade of op-amps to make the pulse readable.

cover.alt: Oscilloscope showing a repeating pulse signal

steps.title: Idea
body: A speaker turns an electrical signal into motion, and the process works in reverse. Press the speaker against skin and the faint beat of the heart moves it up and down, generating a tiny electrical signal.

steps.title: Circuit
body: A cascade of op-amps amplifies that signal until it is large enough to read.

items.alt: Breadboard circuit wired to a small speaker

steps.title: Result
body: The amplified pulse, read on an oscilloscope.

items.alt: Oscilloscope screen showing evenly spaced pulses

projects.title: SinkXSwim
projects.card: A pirate ship survival game built in Godot over one month.
projects.summary: A game built in Godot: you are a pirate with the treasure already on board, and the job is keeping the ship afloat until you get home.

cover.alt: SinkXSwim title screen with a sinking pirate ship

steps.title: Goal
body: After my first semester of college, I wanted to sharpen my programming. I had made two games with Pygame and wanted to try a professional engine.

I picked Godot because it is lightweight and its scripting language is close to Python. I worked through a platformer tutorial and added an item of my own, a banana that boosts jump height for a limited time.

items.cap: Tutorial platformer with my custom banana item
items.alt: Simple platformer level built while learning Godot

steps.title: Game design
body: I wanted the game to feel chaotic, with the player always running to keep things working. Leaks open below deck and spawn garbage that slows you down. You can only carry so much, so you haul it above deck and throw it overboard.
Each leak also drops wood, the resource for repairs. If the game senses you are struggling, there is a rare chance a leak drops duct tape that seals every leak at once.

items.cap: The ship level in the Godot editor
items.alt: Godot editor showing the pirate ship level and game UI

steps.title: Build
body: Over a month I wrote the leak and damage tracking, a progress bar to the destination, animations for the ship breaking and sinking, a title screen, sound effects, and a full tutorial level where a talking parrot shows you how to play.

steps.title: Result
body: One complete level, published as a demo on itch.io. The project put my programming skills back to work and taught me to apply them to something bigger.

items.alt: Itch.io page for the SinkXSwim demo

projects.title: 4-Bar Linkage
projects.kicker: A cat that almost catches a bird
projects.card: A SolidWorks linkage assembly built with McMaster-Carr hardware.
projects.summary: A 4-bar linkage assembly in SolidWorks, built with McMaster-Carr hardware and styled as a cat trying to catch a bird.

steps.title: Goal
body: Learn SolidWorks assemblies, and how to present engineering drawings and bills of materials properly.

steps.title: Motion
body: I tuned the length of each link in an online linkage tool until I had a motion I liked. Then I modeled each piece and assembled them with coincident and rotating mates, and checked that the motion matched.

steps.title: Detail
body: I styled the linkage so it looks like a cat trying to catch a bird, then finished the assembly with screws, nuts, and washers from McMaster-Carr.

projects.title: Temperature Sensor Box
projects.kicker: An alarm for when it gets too hot or too cold
projects.card: An Arduino temperature alarm with a custom 3D printed battery holder.
projects.summary: An Arduino box that monitors the temperature around it and sounds an alarm when it leaves a set range.

steps.title: Build
body: I drilled the enclosure for the speaker, power switch, and LEDs, then recreated the box in CAD to make sure every part would fit. I designed and 3D printed a holder for the 9 V battery, assembled the circuit, and put it all together.

steps.title: Result
body: A working temperature alarm. The project built on things I already knew and expanded my understanding of Arduino, wiring, and how electrical components talk to each other.

projects.title: Laser-Cut Portfolio
projects.card: A physical portfolio book with a laser-cut wooden cover inspired by spider webs.
projects.summary: A physical portfolio book with a laser-cut wooden cover, designed from the geometry of spider webs.

steps.title: Brief
body: Take something from nature and use its geometry in a way that leaves it familiar but distinct. I chose spiders and their webs and started sketching.

steps.title: Digitize
body: I photographed my final sketch, reduced it to black and white in Photoshop, then removed the artifacts by hand in Adobe Illustrator so the laser cutter could read it.

steps.title: Make
body: I laser cut the cover from wood and stained it for a shinier finish that keeps the raw wood look. The book is bound with archival black paper and a plastic spine.

projects.title: FIRST Robotics
projects.kicker: Intake design and a seat at the controls
projects.card: Intake design and driving for my high school FIRST Robotics Competition team.
projects.summary: A season on my high school FIRST Robotics Competition team: I designed the intake, helped build a backup robot, and drove at competition.

steps.title: Intake, version 1
body: A row of rubber wheels on a motor-driven axle. The wheels were not rigid enough to fully pull in the game pieces.

steps.title: Intake, version 2
body: Rubber tubing wrapped around the axle, held by bent metal hanger wire fed through the center. It held extremely well, but the wire made the tube too rigid, the opposite problem.
I shortened the wire and filled the rest with cut zip ties. The center stayed stiff enough to grip the axle and the outer part stayed soft enough to pull the pieces in.

steps.title: Final intake
body: We combined the wheels and the tubing, and had the intake start upright and drop down to deploy so the robot fit the size limit.

steps.title: Competition
body: Last-minute fixes meant my co-driver and I could not practice until the day before. I drove the body of the robot while he ran the intake and end effector. After the season, I built a ball launcher for a game at our club's fair.
